finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token with `==` against an untrusted $token. PHP loose comparison lets a non-string $token authenticate: boolean true equals any non-empty stored string, so a reset can succeed without knowing the token. Numeric-looking tokens can also match via type juggling ("0e..." == "0e...").
finding.source: $token parameter of reset_password_loose (line 2). Attacker-controlled if the caller passes request input without string-typing it, e.g. JSON-decoded `"token": true` or `"token": 0`. The caller is not in this repo, so the precondition is unverified.
finding.sink: Authentication decision at line 4 (`$row['token'] == $token`), followed by the password overwrite at lines 5-6 for the email the attacker names.

trace.note: Function takes $token untyped; no type coercion at entry
Fetches stored token for $email via $db->quote; row may be false if none exists
`if ($row && $row['token'] == $token)`: loose ==, so true == 'anystring' is true and numeric strings compare numerically
Overwrites users.pw with password_hash($new) for the attacker-chosen email

finding.guards_checked: Checked: $row truthiness (lines 4) rejects a missing row only. Checked: $db->quote on $email (lines 3, 6), which prevents SQL injection but not this auth bypass. No type check, no hash_equals, no strict ===. The sibling reset_password() at line 14 uses hash_equals with (string) cast, which is the correct pattern, so the loose variant is the weak one.

verdict.guard_found: Only `$row` truthiness at reset.php:4 (rejects a missing reset row). No type check, strict ===, or hash_equals on the loose path. $db->quote at lines 3, 5-6 prevents SQL injection only. The sibling reset_password() at reset.php:14 uses hash_equals with a (string) cast, but it is a separate function and does not guard reset_password_loose.
verdict.reason: The trace matches the code: reset.php:4 uses loose `==` on `$row['token'] == $token` and reset.php:5-6 overwrites the password, so `true == 'anystring'` (PHP 8) and numeric-string juggling (PHP <8, or "0e..." hashes) would pass the check. Whether an attacker can reach it depends on a caller that is not in this directory (only reset.php exists), so the untrusted, untyped `$token` precondition cannot be confirmed or refuted from the available code.

finding.claim: A reset token is never consumed or expired. On success (lines 7 and 17) the resets row is left in place, and the query at lines 3 and 13 has no expiry condition. A leaked or previously issued token can be replayed to reset the password again at any later time.
finding.source: $token and $email, attacker-supplied. The precondition is possession of a previously valid token for an email, from a leaked reset link, mail-log exposure, or an earlier reset the attacker observed.
finding.sink: Protected operation: the password overwrite at lines 5-6 and 15-16, which is authorized only by the token match.

trace.note: Query selects token for the email with no created_at/expires_at filter
Returns true without DELETE or UPDATE of the resets row, so the token stays valid
reset_password repeats the same query with no expiry filter
Again returns true without invalidating the token

finding.guards_checked: Checked: nothing in this file deletes, marks used, or expires the token. Expiry or single-use may be enforced by the caller or by a DB trigger or job that is not in this repo, so this is unverified. Within this code, no control exists.

verdict.guard_found: none in the repo. reset.php:3 and :13 select the token with no created_at/expires_at filter, and no DELETE or UPDATE of the resets row appears anywhere in the file. The only check is the token comparison at reset.php:4 (==) and :14 (hash_equals), which gates the password write but does not consume or expire the token. The repo contains only reset.php, so a DB trigger or cleanup job outside the repo is unverifiable, but nothing in this code enforces single use or expiry.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: the token query at reset.php:3 and :13 has no expiry filter, the password is overwritten at :5-6 and :15-16, and the function returns true at :7 and :17 without deleting or marking the resets row, so a previously valid token stays usable for a later reset. The attacker must already hold a token for the target email, such as a leaked reset link, which is a real but bounded precondition.

finding.claim: No attempt limiting or lockout on reset-token guessing. Both functions return false with no counter, delay, or logging, so an attacker can brute-force the token online for an email if its entropy is low.
finding.sink: Authentication decision at line 14 (reset_password) and line 4 (reset_password_loose), which gates the password overwrite.

trace.note: Each call issues a fresh SELECT for the email
hash_equals compares the candidate; a mismatch returns false at line 19 with no throttling
